name: Corporate R&D Burn Rate
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Burning the Runway: What It Costs to Chase a Quantum Advantage
lesson.summary: Building and operating a quantum computer consumes enormous amounts of cash every quarter with little offsetting product revenue, and tracking that burn rate is the first step to judging whether a company's public roadmap is realistic.
lesson.body:
Burn rate is a simple idea borrowed from ordinary startup finance: it is the net amount of cash a company spends, above what it brings in, over a given period, usually reported quarterly or annually. Any young, R&D-heavy company burns cash while it builds something, but quantum computing burns cash at an unusual rate even by deep-tech standards, because almost every input is scarce and expensive. The talent pool of physicists and engineers who can design, fabricate, and calibrate qubits is small worldwide, and salaries reflect that scarcity. The hardware itself is exotic: a single dilution refrigerator, the device that cools superconducting qubit chips to near absolute zero, can cost several hundred thousand dollars and sometimes more than a million, and a serious lab needs several, plus custom control electronics, cleanroom fabrication space, or precision laser and vacuum systems for ion trap and photonic approaches.

The cumulative figure of $100 billion or more invested in quantum computing globally, spanning government programs and private capital over roughly the past decade, sounds like a war chest. But that total is a stock, a one-time sum built up over years, while burn rate is a flow, the pace at which individual companies draw that stock down quarter after quarter. Public filings from pure-play quantum companies show annual net losses running into the tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, even at firms with respected roadmaps. The $100 billion headline number and a single company's burn rate answer different questions: one describes how much the field has attracted, the other how fast any one bet inside it is spending down its own resources.

A simple illustration makes the pressure concrete. Suppose a company holds $500 million in cash and burns $150 million a year. Dividing gives roughly three and a third years of runway, the point at which, absent new revenue or a fresh capital raise, the company runs out of cash regardless of how promising its underlying physics looks in a lab notebook. That arithmetic does not care about qubit counts or error rates. It is why deep-tech companies, quantum computing included, face constant pressure to either raise new capital, which usually requires convincing investors that meaningful progress has occurred, or extend runway by cutting costs, which can slow the very research the company was funded to do.

This creates a structural incentive worth watching for, independent of whether any particular scientific claim is true. A company nearing the end of its runway has a strong reason to publicize a milestone, a new qubit count, a benchmark result, a partnership announcement, timed to precede a fundraising round or earnings call, because investor sentiment moves stock prices and access to capital more than quiet, incremental lab progress does. That does not mean every announcement is hollow, but it means announcement timing is not solely a function of scientific readiness.

Understanding burn rate is what lets a skeptical reader separate a company's technical roadmap from its cash roadmap. A hardware architecture might genuinely be ten years from commercial maturity, but the company pursuing it might only have three years of cash. When those two clocks are out of sync, something has to give: a funding round closes, costs get cut, the company gets acquired, or it runs out of money. None of that tells you whether the physics will eventually work, but it tells you which announcements deserve extra scrutiny and why the industry's narrative tends to run ahead of its lab results.
